title: Introduction to Working Capital
shortExplanation: Working capital is the difference between a company's current assets and current liabilities. Under NRB Working Capital Guidelines 2027, banks must assess borrower's working capital cycle, liquidity position, and operating cycle before sanctioning limits. This module introduces the core concept and its importance in credit risk assessment. A proper understanding of working capital helps bankers evaluate the borrower's ability to meet short-term obligations and fund day-to-day operations efficiently.
q1_text: What is the formula for working capital?
q1_explanation: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities. This measures a firm's ability to meet short-term obligations using its short-term assets. A positive figure indicates the company can fund its operations and has buffer for unexpected expenses.
q2_text: Which body regulates working capital lending in Nepal?
q2_explanation: Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) issues directives for working capital lending under the Unified Directives. The latest update incorporates risk-based lending norms and sector-specific exposure limits that banks must follow when sanctioning working capital facilities.
q3_explanation: Positive working capital means current assets exceed current liabilities. This gives the company liquidity to fund operations, pay suppliers, and manage seasonal fluctuations without relying on external borrowing.

title: Classification of Working Capital Loans
shortExplanation: NRB classifies working capital loans into Overdraft (OD) and Cash Credit (CC). OD offers a flexible limit with interest charged only on drawn amount — ideal for seasonal needs. CC is a limit against hypothecation of inventory and receivables. Banks must classify based on business cycle, repayment capacity, and nature of working capital gap. Misclassification can lead to NPA and regulatory penalties under NRB directives.
q1_optionA: Flexible limit with interest on drawn amount
q1_explanation: OD allows drawing up to a sanctioned limit; interest applies only on utilized amount. Best for temporary cash flow gaps and seasonal peaks. NRB mandates that OD limits must be reviewed annually based on actual utilization pattern.
q2_text: What secures a Cash Credit facility?
q2_explanation: CC is a working capital limit secured by hypothecation of current assets — stock, raw materials, and book debts. The borrower retains possession but the bank has a charge over these assets. NRB requires periodic stock audits for CC accounts above Rs. 10 million.
q3_text: Which facility suits seasonal working capital needs?
q3_explanation: Seasonal businesses benefit from OD's flexibility — draw when inventory builds up pre-season, repay when sales generate cash. This matches the actual cash flow cycle better than a fixed CC limit.

title: Introduction to Foreign Exchange Market
shortExplanation: The foreign exchange market (Forex or FX) is the global marketplace for trading currencies. NRB regulates all forex transactions in Nepal under the Foreign Exchange (Regulation) Act. Banks must comply with exchange rate bands, open position limits, and reporting requirements. This module covers market participants, exchange rate mechanisms, and the role of NRB as the monetary authority managing the country's foreign currency reserves.
q1_optionB: A stock exchange for foreign companies
q1_explanation: The forex market is where currencies are traded globally. It is the largest financial market by volume, operating 24 hours a day. In Nepal, all forex transactions must go through NRB-authorized banks at rates within the prescribed bands.
q2_text: Who regulates forex transactions in Nepal?
q2_explanation: NRB is the sole authority regulating forex transactions under the Foreign Exchange (Regulation) Act 2019. It sets the exchange rate band within which authorized dealers (commercial banks) can operate and sets open position limits to manage currency risk.
q3_text: What is an exchange rate band?
q3_optionA: A range within which the currency can trade
q3_optionC: The profit margin on forex trades
q3_explanation: An exchange rate band is the allowable range (upper and lower limit) within which authorized dealers can quote exchange rates. NRB sets these bands to maintain stability and prevent excessive volatility in the Nepalese rupee.

title: Authorized Dealers and Licensing
shortExplanation: Only licensed banks and financial institutions can deal in foreign exchange in Nepal. NRB issues three categories of licenses: 'A' (full forex dealer), 'B' (limited dealing — Travelers Cheques and remittance only), and 'C' (money transfer only). Each category has distinct capital requirements, reporting obligations, and transaction limits. This chapter covers the licensing framework, eligibility criteria, and compliance requirements for authorized dealers.
q1_text: How many license categories does NRB issue for forex dealing?
q1_explanation: NRB issues three license categories: 'A' for full forex dealing (all transactions), 'B' for limited dealing (TCs and remittance), and 'C' for money transfer only. Each has different capital requirements — 'A' requires the highest paid-up capital.
q2_text: What can a 'B' category licensee do?
q2_explanation: 'B' license holders can deal in Travelers Cheques and inward/outward remittance only. They cannot open letters of credit, handle import/export payments, or maintain foreign currency accounts. These activities are reserved for 'A' category dealers.
q3_text: What is a key compliance requirement for authorized dealers?
q3_optionA: Submit daily transaction reports to NRB
q3_explanation: Authorized dealers must submit daily forex transaction reports to NRB's reporting system. This includes purchase/sale amounts, counterparties, and exchange rates applied. NRB uses this data to monitor market activity and ensure compliance with open position limits.
